newsitem.title: UK: Labour heads for record British election victory.
newsitem.headline: Labour heads for record British election victory.

text.p: Tony Blair's Labour party was set on Thursday to end 18 years of Conservative rule in Britain with a landslide election victory on a scale unseen since 1832.
Exit polls by Britain's two main television news broadcasters, released as voting ended at 2100 GMT, projected that Labour would have a huge majority in the 659-seat parliament of more than 150.
ITN said Labour could have a majority of 159 seats on a swing to Labour from the Conservatives of 12.2 percent.
The BBC's exit polls gave Labour 47 percent support, 29 percent for the Conservatives and 18 percent for the centre-left Liberal Democrats. It said the majority could be nearer to 200.
"A number of people thought it couldn't happen but if it does, Labour will have its largest majority ever, the Conservatives will have their lo
Conservatives will have their lowest share of the vote since at least 1859 -- an historic night indeed," political professor Colin Rallings told ITN.

Politicians reacted cautiously, as if unable to believe that the actual results, most of which will be announced overnight, would confirm the huge opinion poll lead that Labour carved out and then maintained during a gruelling six-week campaign.
"I am sure these exit polls are exaggerated, but it does look like a good win and obviously I am very pleased," Peter Mandelson, who organised Labour's campaign, told ITN.

Leading Conservatives hoped the margin of defeat would be narrower than the polls suggested but Lord Jeffrey Archer, a close friend of Prime Minister John Major, was the first to concede defeat and congratulate Blair.
Labour, which lost the four preceding elections, stormed to power in 1945 with a 144-seat majority. Anything greater than that would be the biggest victory since 1832.
"There has been nothing like it this century. It is a like an asteroid destroying practically all life on earth," politics professor Anthony King said.
The first result to be announced was in the safe Labour seat of Sunderland South, which Chris Mullin held with an increased majority on a swing from the Conservatives of 10.5 percent.

If the swing is repeated across the country, it will represent a ringing endorsement for Blair's crusade, since he became Labour leader three years ago, to dump the party's socialist baggage and reposition it in the political centre.
"This is much the biggest thing that has happened since the war to any party in any election. This is a turnover of monumental scale," Oxford academic David Butler said.
Blair, 43, would be the youngest prime minister this century. He was a student at Oxford University when Labour last won a British election in 1974.
Defeat for Major, who defied polls to come from behind to win the 1992 election, would mark the end of the longest period of single-party government this century in Britain.

Over 18 years, first under "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher and then under Major, the Conservatives turned Britain upside down, halting decades of relative economic decline by privatising vast swathes of industry and taming powerful trade unions.
But critics said the price of greater economic efficiency was too high, with the gap between rich and poor widening more than in any other developed country except New Zealand.

In the course of a gruelling but largely uneventful campaign, Blair hammered home his argument that Britain had become a less fair, less decent society and promised to turn it into a country "for the many, not the few".

Major's appeal to voters was "better the devil you know than the devil you don't", but deep divisions over Europe, broken promises over tax and allegations of sleaze in the ruling party meant he had a Herculean task.
Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, a likely contender in any future Conservative leadership fight, admitted that infighting over Europe had damged the Conservatives.
"We don't know what the result was, but I'm sure the Conservatives would have done better if they had been united in the past few years," he said.
